sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot vii (printed pp. 47–55)
rows: [p. 47] [Margin: Nodus VII. Demonstratio Aristotelis pro Immortalitate Coeli.] Asphal. At nisi quicquam praefers, quam toties commemorasti demonstrationem, et quantum valeat, et quo deficiat, expende. Andabatae, licet iam perito, mei causa, audire non erit ingratum.

[p. 47] [Margin: Knot VII. Demonstration [demonstratio] of Aristotle for the Immortality of the Heaven.] Asphal. But unless you prefer anything [else], the demonstration which you have so often mentioned, both how much it is worth [valeat] and in what it falls short [deficiat], weigh [expende]. To Andabata, although already skilled [perito], for my sake, it will not be unwelcome [ingratum] to hear [it].

Ereu. Demonstratio talis est. Lineae simplices recta sunt et circularis; Motus vero simplices, qui supra lineas simplices fiunt. Motus itaque incompositi naturales totidem erunt; et ea corpora simplicia quae his secundum naturam feruntur. Iam habes Coelum corpus simplex, postquam simplici motu fertur, et distinctum ab iis quae recta feruntur. Nunc rectos motus intuere oppositos, secundum rectam lineam enim ab utrovis termino, in reliquum possibilis est motus, et in natura terminos habemus Centrum et circumferentiam; motus autem Circularis nullo fine in seipsum semper revertitur.

Ereu. The demonstration is such. Simple lines are the straight and the circular; but simple motions, [those] which are made upon simple lines. The uncompounded [incompositi] natural motions therefore will be as many [totidem]; and those [are] simple bodies which are borne [feruntur] by these according to nature. Now you have the Heaven a simple body, since [postquam] it is borne by a simple motion, and distinct from those which are borne straight [recta]. Now look upon [intuere] the straight motions [as] opposite; for according to a straight line, from either end [termino], into the other [reliquum] motion is possible, and in nature we have [as] ends [terminos] the Centre and the circumference; but the Circular motion with no end [fine] always returns into itself.

Contrarii itaque sunt motus recti [p. 48] et inimici, et corpora itaque, quae his secundum naturam motibus utuntur, sibi invicem malum et destructionem meditantur. Liberum coelum eorum furias immuni ab eorum minis volatu, et continet et ridet, aeternitatem sibi, motus connaturalis perpetuitate, essentiam proportionatam et indicantis et sibi vindicantis, usurpans.

Contrary therefore are the straight motions [p. 48] and hostile [inimici], and the bodies therefore, which use these motions according to nature, plot [meditantur] evil and destruction for one another. The free heaven, with a flight immune from their threats, both restrains [continet] and laughs at their furies, usurping [usurpans] for itself eternity by the perpetuity of a connatural motion, [a motion] both indicating and claiming [vindicantis] for itself a proportioned essence [essentiam proportionatam].
Hanc demonstrationis summam, ipsa, ut vides, facie venerandam, si examinari iubes, hoc primum interrogo. Unde constet Circularem lineam esse simplicem?
This sum of the demonstration, venerable, as you see, by its very face [facie], if you bid [it] to be examined, this I ask first: Whence is it established [constet] that the Circular line is simple?

[Margin: Lineam circularem esse compositam.] Ego vero compositam et decompositam securus affirmo: Linea enim longitudo est, longitudinis autem ratio multiplicatur, et una ad perpendiculum alteri adiungitur, ut superficies nascatur. Ipsa autem longitudo perhibetur nata ex fluxu, seu motu puncti. Hoc itaque primum cogita, punctum quod duarum longitudinum participatione fluit, fluxum habere compositiorem, quam si unam sequeretur: et sicut diametrum parallelogrammi, ex motu utriusque lateris, sic quamcumque curvam ex duabus longitudinibus essentialiter generari: Diametri enim accidentalis est ad latera ratio, quatenus huic rectae contingit esse diametrum: linea autem curva (quoniam exit extra umbram suorum punctorum) ex necessitate latitudinem aeque atque longitudinem in sese includit.

[Margin: That the circular line is composite.] I for my part [vero] securely affirm [it] composite and decomposite [decompositam]: for a line is length [longitudo], but the reason [ratio] of length is multiplied, and one is joined to another at the perpendicular [ad perpendiculum], so that a surface is born. But length itself is held [perhibetur] [to be] born from the flux [fluxu], or motion, of a point. This therefore consider first: that a point which flows by participation of two lengths has a more composite flux than if it followed one; and that, as the diagonal [diametrum] of a parallelogram [is generated] from the motion of each side, so any curve whatever is generated essentially from two lengths. For of the diagonal the relation [ratio] to the sides is accidental, inasmuch as it happens [contingit] to this straight [line] to be a diagonal; but a curved line (since it goes out beyond the shadow [umbram] of its own points) of necessity includes within itself breadth equally as [much as] length.

Duas habes longitudines in cir- [p. 49] culari clausas, tertiam quoque accipito. Nonne vides lineas rectas non minus tres, spatium concludere? claudit autem aream circulus; tribus itaque rectis aequivalet, vel potius quatuor. Recta enim linea reflexione frangitur, fiuntque duae ex una. Esto itaque ex centro A. circulus clausus quadrato, [Margin: Quaere in Tabula figuram I.] et concipiatur punctum D. fluere participando D,A, et D,E, usque ad punctum F, et quoniam ab F, redit versus D,A, ad quam etiam pertingit in puncto G, patet quod motus ipsius participat tertiam lineam B,G: Et rursus, quoniam a puncto G, fit reflexio versus D, ubi finitur circulus, patet circulum quartae lineae H,C, aequivalere. Quid ni et quintae? postquam in puncto I. nova fit reflexio versus A. Sed neque dum finita est circuli compositura.

You have two lengths enclosed in the cir- [p. 49] cular [line]; take [accipito] a third also. Do you not see that straight lines, not fewer [than] three, enclose a space? but the circle encloses an area; therefore it is equivalent to three straight [lines], or rather four. For a straight line is broken by reflexion, and two are made out of one. Let there be therefore, from the centre A, a circle enclosed by a square, [Margin: Look for figure I in the Table.] and let the point D be conceived to flow by participating [in] D,A and D,E as far as the point F; and since from F it returns towards D,A, which also it reaches at the point G, it is plain [patet] that its motion participates [in] a third line B,G. And again, since from the point G a reflexion is made towards D, where the circle is ended, it is plain that the circle is equivalent to a fourth line H,C. Why not also to a fifth? since at the point I a new reflexion is made towards A. But not even yet [neque dum] is the composition [compositura] of the circle finished.

Cum enim motui accidant velocitas et tarditas; motus simplex toto se unam velocitatem habet: qui autem plures habet, compositus est. Circularis autem non sicut diameter quadrati ad utrumque latus eandem proportionem servat, neque sicut diameter parallelogrammi unam ad unum latus, aliam ad reliquum, sed perpetuo mutat proportionem suam. Vides enim a puncto D, usque ad punctum K, maiorem esse velocitatem cursus secundum lineam D,E, quam secundum lineam D,A, et si continuo minorem et minorem habeat pro- [p. 50] portionem, a puncto autem K, usque dum occurrat lineae F,A, velocitatem esse maiorem secundum lineam D A, crescente semper proportione, et hoc per singulos quadrantes observari. Vide modo quam simplicem nobis lineam elegerit, cuius si legem sequatur coelum, omnium Entium erit compositissimum.

For since speed [velocitas] and slowness [tarditas] befall [accidant] motion, a simple motion has through its whole self [toto se] one speed; but that which has more [than one] is composite. But the Circular does not, as the diagonal of a square, keep the same proportion to each side, nor, as the diagonal of a parallelogram, one to one side, another to the other, but perpetually changes its proportion. For you see that from the point D as far as the point K the speed of the course is greater according to the line D,E than according to the line D,A, even if [et si] it has a continually lesser and lesser pro- [p. 50] portion; but from the point K, until it meets the line F,A, that the speed is greater according to the line D A, the proportion always growing; and that this is observed through the single quadrants. See now how simple a line he has chosen for us, whose law if the heaven follows, it will be the most composite of all Beings [Entium].

[Margin: Neque motum rectum Elementis, neque circularem Coelis esse proprium.] Sed quae his motibus feruntur corpora esse simplicia unde notum? Ex eo (inquit) quod natura principium est motus et quietis; unde omni corpori naturali, etiam aliquis motus secundum naturam est, atque proinde necesse est ex motu, tanquam vel fine, vel passione, corporis indolem agnosci. In quibus hoc se se prae caeteris offert, ut quid naturae nomine et motus naturalis intelligendum sit, indagemus. Natura enim alia est communis, alia particularis; et in plantis quidem et animalibus sicut particulares motus sic et instrumenta vel certe determinatas vias horum motuum conspicamur. Hos itaque motus his corporibus speciali et priva naturae qualitate, naturales dicere ipsa nos res monet. Verum in corporibus primis, immo neque in mixtis homogeneis aliquam naturae dispositionem ad hunc motum magis quam illum intuemur. Manet itaque neque ullam nobis rationem suggeri, cur hunc motum ex proprio naturae specialis instinctu, et non magis ex universi dispositione, [p. 51] quae est magnae naturae ratio, deberi existimemus.

[Margin: That neither straight motion is proper to the Elements, nor circular to the Heavens.] But that the bodies which are borne by these motions are simple, whence [is it] known? From this (he says), that nature is the principle [principium] of motion and rest; whence to every natural body also some motion is according to nature, and accordingly it is necessary that from motion, as either from end [fine] or from passion [passione], the disposition [indolem] of the body be recognised. In which [matters] this offers itself before the rest: that we track down [indagemus] what is to be understood by the name of nature and of natural motion. For nature is one [kind] common, another particular; and in plants indeed and animals, as [we behold] particular motions, so also we behold instruments, or at least determinate ways, of these motions. These motions therefore the thing itself warns [monet] us to call natural to these bodies by a special and private [priva] quality of nature. But in the first bodies, nay not even in homogeneous mixed [bodies], do we behold any disposition of nature to this motion more than to that. It remains [Manet] therefore that neither is any reason [rationem] suggested to us why we should think this motion to be owed [deberi] from the proper instinct of a special nature, and not rather from the disposition of the universe, [p. 51] which is the reason [ratio] of the great nature.

Non enim patet naturam ipsorum magis quam naturam communem, hunc eis motum conferre. Deinde alios in his motus magis speciales experimur. Ignem comburere, aquam humectare, ventum exsiccare, terram infrigidare cernimus. Certe Aristoteles singulis elementis duas qualitates motus vel effectrices vel susceptrices donavit. Hi ergo motus erunt ex quibus eorum natura dignoscenda erit, non illi communes.

For it is not plain that their own nature, more than the common nature, confers this motion on them. Next, we experience [experimur] in these other motions more special. We discern [cernimus] fire to burn, water to moisten, wind to dry, earth to chill. Certainly Aristotle gave to the single elements two qualities, either effective [effectrices] or receptive [susceptrices] of motion [motus]. These therefore will be the motions from which their nature will have to be discerned, not those common ones.

Sed neque experimentis constans aliqua fides colligitur: Aquam enim et aerem motu circulari ferri tantum non manibus tangimus. Ignem narrant Peripatetici, eodem cieri; de Terra disputatur, et si coelos credimus circulariter ferri, credimus, non scimus; Si enim haec monstra Excentricorum et Epicyclorum invisibilium vana sint, Astra necesse est non circulo cieri, sed vago vel anomalo quodam motu. De Luna certum est pluribus agitari viis: Iovis et Saturni Satellites accedunt testes.

But neither is any constant faith [fides] gathered from experiments: for that water and air are borne by a circular motion we all but [tantum non] touch with our hands. Fire, the Peripatetics relate, is moved [cieri] by the same; about the Earth there is dispute; and if we believe the heavens to be borne circularly, we believe, we do not know; for if these monsters of invisible Excentrics and Epicycles are vain, it is necessary that the Stars are moved not in a circle, but by some wandering [vago] or anomalous motion. Of the Moon it is certain that it is driven [agitari] by several ways [viis]: the Satellites of Jupiter and Saturn come in [accedunt] as witnesses.

[Margin: Mobile in puncto reflexionis quiescere.] Superest an motus circularis aeternitatem polliceatur, investigemus. Sed si recta sunt quae de compositione circuli diximus, ipse Stagirita non permittet. Docet enim in puncto reflectionis necessariam esse quietem et intervallum inter duos motus: quare cum in decursu circuli quarto reflexionem patiatur mobile, quater [p. 52] in eo decursu interruptus erit motus, quaerendaeque toties causae cur repetatur.

[Margin: That the mobile rests in the point of reflexion.] It remains that we investigate whether circular motion promises eternity. But if the things which we said about the composition of the circle are right, the Stagirite himself will not permit [it]. For he teaches that in the point of reflection [reflectionis] rest and an interval between two motions are necessary: wherefore, since in the running-course [decursu] of a circle the mobile suffers reflexion four times [quarto], four times [p. 52] in that course will the motion be interrupted, and so often are causes to be sought why it is repeated.
Andab. Antiquata iam est haec sententia, neque quisquam est liberioris ingenii qui eam propugnare sustineat.
Andab. This opinion [sententia] has now been antiquated [antiquata], nor is there anyone of a freer wit [ingenii] who would endure [sustineat] to defend it.

Ereu. Sed quo iure tu videris; nisi enim quietem admittant, contrarios motus continuos esse, necesse est fateantur, et quod sequitur, numero indivisos; duo enim instantia in tempore coniungi nequire; sed et subiectum unum esse non ignoras. Deinde cum contraria sint quae sub eodem genere maxime distant, ab uno ad aliud sine medio transitum fieri admittendum est.

Ereu. But by what right [iure], you will see [tu videris]; for unless they admit rest, it is necessary that they confess the contrary motions to be continuous, and, what follows, undivided in number [numero indivisos]; for that two instants cannot be joined in time, and also that the subject is one, you are not ignorant. Next, since contraries are [those] which under the same kind [genere] are most distant, it must be admitted that a transit is made from one to the other without a middle [sine medio].
Asphal. Nosti tamen etiam Galilaeum hanc Aristotelis definitionem impatienter ferre.
Asphal. You know, however, that Galileo too bears impatiently this definition [definitionem] of Aristotle.

Ereu. Novi equidem, et his quae Andabatae opposui, non iri permotum, magis quam ipsus experimentis quae promittit, cessurus sim, nisi forte non sit inter nos vera concertatio. Nescio enim quam notabilem et sensibilem moram expectat Galilaeus, quam Aristoteles non asserit: Metaphysicae enim rationi quaelibet minima mora satisfacit: Experimenta vero non intercedere exiguam aliquam nunquam prodent, vel ipso Galilaeo authore, qui cum inter quietem, et quemlibet determinatum velocitatis gradum, infinitos minores, et mino- [p. 53] res interesse asseruerit, non poterit negare eosdem inter quemlibet determinatum gradum motus ad signum, et motus ab eodem signo bis reperiri. Necessum itaque fit tarditatem aliquam circa ipsum signum omnem sensum motus effugere et favere Aristoteli.

Ereu. I know [it] indeed, and [I know] that he will not be moved by these [things] which I opposed to Andabata, more than I would yield to his [ipsus] experiments which he promises, unless perhaps there is not a true contest [concertatio] between us. For I do not know what notable and sensible delay [moram] Galileo expects which Aristotle does not assert: for to a Metaphysical reason [rationi] any smallest delay whatever satisfies; but experiments will never betray [prodent] that some exiguous [delay] does not intervene, even by Galileo himself as author, who, since he has asserted that between rest and any determinate degree of speed infinite lesser and less- [p. 53] er [degrees] are between, will not be able to deny that the same are found twice between any determinate degree of motion to a mark [signum] and of motion from the same mark. It becomes necessary [Necessum] therefore that some slowness around the mark itself escapes all sense of motion and favours Aristotle.
Asphal. De ipsa vero re quid censes esse moram vel non esse?
Asphal. But about the thing itself, what do you judge [censes]: that there is a delay, or that there is not?

Ereu. Constans est unum saltem esse temporis individuum, quo neque hac, neque illac feratur; ac proinde in eo statu, sit ac si quievisset ante subsequentem motum. Si itaque vis ad quietum accedens immediate illud loco movet, nulla erit quies; sin tempore opus est ad quodlibet movendum quantumlibet exiguo motu, sequetur in puncto reflexionis intervenire quietem. Quoniam autem quae ratio cogit motum in principio esse tardum, eadem neque densitatem quamlibet sine tempore patietur superari, fiet quietem aliquam inter motoris applicationem et mobilis cessionem ex necessitate contingere; quare quietem in reflexionis puncto esse necessariam.

Ereu. It is constant [Constans est] that there is at least one individual [individuum] of time in which it is borne neither this way nor that; and accordingly, in that state, it is as if it had rested before the subsequent motion. If therefore the force [vis] approaching to the [thing] at rest moves it immediately from its place, there will be no rest; but if there is need of time for moving anything whatever by a motion however exiguous, it will follow that in the point of reflexion rest intervenes. But since the same reason [ratio] which compels motion to be slow in [its] beginning [principio] will also not [neque] suffer any density whatever to be overcome without time, it will come about that some rest occurs of necessity between the application of the mover and the yielding [cessionem] of the mobile; wherefore that rest in the point of reflexion is necessary.
Andab. Ergo si pilae a puero eiectae molaris e Luna occurret, tu subsistere molarem vel lentissime ferri credis dum pila cedere dubitabit?

Andab. Then if a millstone [molaris] from the Moon shall meet a ball thrown by a boy, do you believe that the millstone stands still [subsistere] or is borne most slowly while the ball hesitates [dubitabit] to yield?

Ereu. Aer pilae ante molarem occurret cui tantum deferes, Andabata, ut primo certe oc- [p. 54] cursu pilae aliquantulum cedat: et quoniam nullo determinato spatio opus est, dum molaris accedit, iam pilam anteambulonem nacta fuerit. Quare cernitis quomodo nihil de tota demonstratione adeo celebri certi constantisque reliquum sit.

Ereu. The air will meet the ball before the millstone, [the air] to which you will grant [deferes] so much, Andabata, that at the first meet- [p. 54] ing at least it yields somewhat to the ball; and since there is need of no determinate space, while the millstone approaches, it will already have got [nacta fuerit] the ball as a forerunner [anteambulonem]. Wherefore you [pl.] discern how nothing certain and constant is left of the whole demonstration, so celebrated.
Asphal. Hui! quam formosam nobis speciem decalvasti? sed si memini, vim in ea aliquam subindicabas, neque omni prorsus robore destitutam.

Asphal. Whew [Hui]! how fair an appearance [speciem] you have made bald [decalvasti] for us! But, if I remember, you were hinting [subindicabas] some force in it, and [it] not utterly destitute of all strength [robore].

Ereu. Est ut dicis, haec siquidem certa sunt. Et elementa sursum deorsumque ferri, et Astra circulo moveri. Utrumque hunc motum et ipsorum differentias animo metientibus, hoc evidens fit, tam diversos motus non nisi ex diversis naturae, et ipsius parentis circa haec corpora dispositionibus illis esse attributos. Hoc persequentes necessum est in illud devenire, elementa per hos motus, permutationem continuam et mixtionem subire. Manifestum itaque fit hos motus ad generationem et corruptionem, quae mixtione perficiuntur, pertinere.

Ereu. It is as you say, since these things indeed are certain: both that the elements are borne upward and downward, and that the Stars are moved in a circle. To [those] measuring in mind each of these motions and their differences, this becomes evident: that motions so diverse have not been attributed to them except from diverse dispositions of nature, and of the parent itself, concerning these bodies. Pursuing this, it is necessary to arrive at that: that the elements through these motions undergo continual permutation and mixtion [mixtionem]. It becomes manifest therefore that these motions pertain to generation and corruption, which are perfected by mixtion.

Reliquum motum, si cur fiat, minime percipiamus, certe ex stato ordine corporumque circulo motorum distantia hoc percipimus, ad globos illos Astrorum in sua temperie conservandos eam remotionem et volutationem spectare. Hoc itaque his e motibus arguitur: et particularium apud [p. 55] nos esse generationem et corruptionem, et ingentium corporum illorum non esse. An vero ingentium illorum corporum decisae particulae easdem aut similes nostris permutationum leges subeant, nihil ex eorum motuum sic in universum consideratorum conditione colligi posse.

The remaining motion, if we should least perceive why it is made, certainly from the fixed [stato] order and the distance of the bodies moved in a circle we perceive this: that that removal [remotionem] and rolling [volutationem] looks [spectare] to the preserving of those globes of the Stars in their temperament [temperie]. This therefore is argued from these motions: both that there is generation and corruption of particulars among [p. 55] us, and that there is not [of] those huge bodies. But whether particles cut off [decisae] from those huge bodies undergo the same laws of permutations as ours, or similar, nothing [of that] can be gathered from the condition of their motions thus considered in general [in universum].
Andab. Mirum ni Ereunius noster Dominicum Consalvum alitem illum veredarium post nuperrimum de Luna ad nos iter convenerit, adeo secure de iis quae in coelis aguntur, narrat.

Andab. A wonder if [Mirum ni] our Ereunius has not met Dominicus Consalvus [Domingo Gonsales], that winged courier [alitem illum veredarium], after his most recent journey from the Moon to us, so securely does he narrate about the things which are done in the heavens.

Ereu. Tam cito irrides Andabata? At cum neque morti neque tactui corpora haec subiecta crederentur, et innumera praeterea incredibilia adderentur, facili fide capiebas, neque vel probationem poscebas. Nunc postquam similia eorum quae vides et tangis loquimur, neque aperta demonstratio neque eorum quae contra afferebantur, dissolutio, neque tanti erroris patefacta origo, etsi Christiano nomini pudenda, quicquam te movere possunt. [Knot viii follows on p. 55.]

Ereu. So quickly do you mock, Andabata? But when these bodies were believed subject neither to death nor to touch, and innumerable incredible things besides were added, you took [them] with easy faith, nor did you even [vel] demand proof. Now, after we speak things similar to those which you see and touch, neither an open demonstration, nor the dissolution of those [things] which were brought against [it], nor the origin of so great an error laid open, although shameful to the Christian name, can move you at all [quicquam]. [Knot viii follows on p. 55.]

terms: Demonstration of Aristotle for the Immortality of the Heaven
FM2 table title: 'de natura Coeli' ('on the nature of the Heaven').
Aristotle, De caelo I.2–3: simple lines → simple motions → simple bodies; circular motion has no contrary, so the heaven is ungenerated and incorruptible.
lineae simplices / motus simplices / corpora simplicia
simple lines / simple motions / simple bodies
De caelo I.2, 268b17ff.: only straight and circular lines are simple. White attacks the first premise.
White claims the circle is not merely composite but doubly so.
Kinematic generation of magnitudes (Proclus; Barrow later): a line is the flux of a point.
Classical usage: the diagonal of a quadrilateral. The diagonal as the resultant of two side-motions is the parallelogram of motions (pseudo-Aristotle, Mechanica 1).
Obscure image: a curve leaves the line of its points, so it has breadth; perhaps from Digby's or White's projection-language.
Rare, late Latin; kept distinct from compositio.
Aristotelian accidents of motion; a 'simple' motion should have a single speed.
White means the changing ratio of the components of circular motion along two perpendicular axes.
Cf. glossary; used of the inner nature of a body known from its motion.
as either from end or from passion
Scholastic: motion reveals nature either as its goal or as its proper affection.
Distinction between the order of the whole universe and the nature of a single species; White ascribes the elements' 'natural' motions to the universe's disposition.
Aristotle, De gen. et corr. II.2–3: hot and cold active, wet and dry passive; each element has two.
Ptolemaic devices; White calls them invisible 'monsters'.
Galileo's Medicean stars (1610) and his 'tricorporeal' Saturn (the rings read as two companions), taken as evidence that heavenly bodies move along several paths.
rest in the point of reflexion
Aristotle, Physics VIII.8, 262a–b: a body reversing its motion must stop. Galileo rejected the necessity of a sensible pause (Dialogo, Day 1 and Two New Sciences).
If contrary motions are continuous without rest, they become one numerical motion, which Aristotle denies.
contraria (quae sub eodem genere maxime distant)
contraries (which under the same kind are most distant)
Aristotle's definition of contraries (Categories 6a17; Metaph. X.4).
archaic form of 'ipse'; here probably a misprint for 'ipsius'.
Here the turning-point of a motion.
= an indivisible of time, an instant.
Echoes the reductio used against quies media: a ball thrown up would stop a falling great body (cf. Galileo, Dialogo, Day 1). Treated as feminine ('nacta').
Rare late-Latin verb; the 'fair appearance' of the demonstration is stripped of its hair.
ales = bird / winged one; veredarius = post-rider.
Hero of Francis Godwin's The Man in the Moone (1638), carried to the Moon by wild swans (gansas); joke on Ereunius' confident knowledge of the heavens.
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot vii, complete in one part. PDF pp. 58–66 = printed pp. 47–55. Begins on p. 47 with Asphalius' 'At nisi quicquam praefers' (margin 'Nodus VII. Demonstratio Aristotelis pro Immortalitate Coeli'; FM2 lists it as 'Demonstratio Aristotelis de natura Coeli', p. 47) and ends on p. 55 with Ereunius' '…quicquam te movere possunt.' Knot viii (margin 'Nodus VIII. In Coelis esse corpora Analoga nostris') begins on p. 55 at Andabata's 'Ergo te demonstravisse dicis' (PDF 66), as FM2 says. Offset +11 holds (p. 55 = PDF 66).

Rows: one per speech; Ereunius' long speeches split at sentence or paragraph breaks; printed page breaks marked [p. n] (including mid-word breaks, e.g. 'cir- [p. 49] culari'). Four marginal notes besides the knot title, placed where they stand.

Conventions as in glossary.md. Printed 'Consaluum' normalized to 'Consalvum' (consonantal u → v). Spellings kept as printed: 'reflectionis' beside 'reflexionis'; 'ipsus'; 'Necessum'; 'quatuor'; 'authore'; 'expectat'.

Readings: (a) p. 49 margin is printed 'Quare in Tabula figuram I.'; read as 'Quaere' (look for), since 'quare' gives no sense; the figure is Figure I of the Tabula figurarum (FM2). (b) p. 51 'quarto reflexionem patiatur' — 'quarto' (adv.) literally 'for the fourth time'; the sense ('four times', cf. following 'quater') is given with the Latin bracketed. (c) p. 52 'ipsus' is probably a misprint for 'ipsius'. (d) p. 54 'nacta fuerit': the feminine participle has no feminine subject unless 'molaris' is taken as feminine (as if 'mola'); translated with 'the millstone' as subject. (e) p. 53 'Necessum itaque fit' – old form of necesse. No illegible words.

Interpretation: the geometry of p. 49 (points D, E, F, G, H, I, K and lines B,G, H,C) refers to Figure I of the Tabula; the reflexion count is White's own and is translated without correction. 'Saturni Satellites' refers to Galileo's 1610 observation of Saturn as 'tricorporeal'. The millstone/ball example is the classic objection to Aristotle's quies media. (f) p. 54 'dispositionibus illis' — 'illis' may be dative ('attributed to them', as translated) or agree with 'dispositionibus' ('those dispositions').

Verification pass: the Latin was re-checked against the page images and the English against the Latin sentence by sentence (cases, tenses, moods, agreement, negatives, comparatives, omissions). It produced 4 corrections: (1) the margin 'Quaere in Tabula figuram I.' moved to its printed position beside 'circulus clausus quadrato' (first placed after 'aequivalere'); (2) the missing page break [p. 54] inserted in 'oc- [p. 54] cursu'; (3) 'Consaluum' normalized to 'Consalvum' per the u/v convention; (4) the ambiguity of 'illis' (p. 54) added to the notes. Points settled while drafting and re-confirmed: 'indicantis … vindicantis' agree with genitive 'motus', not with the heaven; 'velocitatem esse maiorem' and 'hoc … observari' remain governed by 'Vides'; 'neque … patietur' = 'will also not suffer'.
